summary.short: Proposed bill amending Article 92 of Uruguay's Law No. 19.580 to penalise unauthorised disclosure of real or AI-simulated intimate images or recordings, with six months to two years' imprisonment. Website, portal and search-engine administrators must remove such content immediately once notified, under the same penalty; no start date stated.
summary.long: Single-article bill (Carpeta 691/2025, July 2025) replacing Article 92 of Law No. 19.580. Paragraph 1 criminalises whoever disseminates, discloses, exhibits or transfers to third parties real or simulated images or recordings of a person with intimate or sexual content without authorisation, punishable by six months to two years' imprisonment ('prisión' to 'penitenciaría'). Paragraph 2 defines simulated images as those created by artificial intelligence, digital editing or other technology producing a false but credible representation of a person's appearance, voice or conduct. Paragraph 3 states that authorisation given by a person under eighteen is never valid, and that the offence applies even if the disseminator took part in the recordings. Paragraph 4 applies the same penalty to administrators of websites, portals, search engines or similar services who, once notified of the lack of authorisation, do not remove the images immediately. The explanatory memorandum cites deepfake abuse mainly affecting women and minors and foreign measures; it says the bill would also penalise creation and modification, which the operative wording does not expressly cover. No entry-into-force date is stated.

notes: Single-article bill (Artículo único), Carpeta Nº 691/2025, Repartido Nº 346, July 2025, as submitted; not a consolidated text. The registry title's reference to 'violencia hacia las mujeres basada en género' does not appear in the bill text; the document is authoritative. Internal points: the exposición de motivos describes 'mínimos cambios' to the existing law, while the replacement article adds a definition of simulated images and a liability clause for site administrators. The administrator clause refers back to the same article for its penalty ('la misma pena prevista en este artículo'). The text states no penalty amounts beyond the prison terms in art. 92. The exposición de motivos cites the US Take It Down Act, Spain, Germany, France, Canada and the UK Online Safety Act as comparators only; these are not coded as relations. Site administrators, portals and search engines are addressees as a class, not named entities.

obligations.summary: Administrators of internet sites, portals, search engines or similar services, once notified of the lack of authorization, must take down the images or recordings immediately. The same article's fourth paragraph attaches a criminal sanction to failure to do so, which is recorded here only as the duty's trigger, not as a separate enforcement entry. The bill's other operative provisions (the offence in the first paragraph, the definition of simulated images, and the rule that consent given by a person under eighteen is not valid) are not coded as obligations.
